title: Secret Number Notes
story: Two friends pass notes in a simple code: each letter becomes its alphabet position (A is 1, Z is 26), and the numbers are written together with no spaces. "KZ" becomes 1126.
But 1126 could also be "AABF", "ALF" and more. Before guessing, the reader wants to know how many messages a note could mean.
task: Write countReadings(note). note is a string of digits. Split it into pieces, each a number from 1 to 26 written without a leading zero, and return how many different splits there are.
So "10" and "20" are valid pieces, but "0", "05" and "27" are not. If the note cannot be split at all, return 0.
constraints: note contains only the digits 0 to 9.

examples.explanation: The splits are 1-1-2-6 (AABF), 11-2-6 (KBF), 1-12-6 (ALF), 1-1-26 (AAZ) and 11-26 (KZ). 126 is too big, so nothing else works.
A 0 cannot stand alone, so it must end a 10 or 20. Here it pairs with the 1, forcing 2-10-5 (BJE). The split 21-0-5 fails on the lone 0.

hints: The last piece of any reading of 1126 is either 6 or 26. What is left of the note in each case?
The rest is 112 or 11. Every reading of the full note is a reading of one of those prefixes plus the last piece. So you only need counts for shorter prefixes.
Let ways[i] be the number of readings of the first i digits, with ways[0] = 1. Add ways[i - 1] when digit i alone is 1 to 9. Add ways[i - 2] when the last two digits form 10 to 26.
Fill ways left to right. Watch the zeros: a single 0 adds nothing, and a pair starting with 0 (like 05) is not 10 to 26, so it adds nothing either. Only the last two values are needed.
bruteForce: Recursively cut one or two digits off the front, check the piece, and count splits that reach the end. Correct, but a note of sixty 1s has about 2.5 trillion readings, and the recursion walks every one.
Most of that work is repeated. The number of readings of the rest of the note from position 30 is the same however the recursion got there, yet it recomputes that number for every path.

js: * @param {string} note  digits written with no spaces
* @return {number} number of ways to read it as letters 1-26

tests.note: leading zero is not a letter
30 is too big and 0 cannot stand alone
longest note: needs DP, not plain recursion

js: let prev2 = 1; // readings of the prefix two digits back (empty prefix: 1)
let prev1 = note[0] === "0" ? 0 : 1; // readings of the first digit
if (note[i] !== "0") here += prev1;         // last piece is one digit
if (pair >= 10 && pair <= 26) here += prev2; // last piece is two digits
py: prev2 = 1  # readings of the prefix two digits back (empty prefix: 1)
prev1 = 0 if note[0] == "0" else 1  # readings of the first digit
here += prev1  # last piece is one digit
here += prev2  # last piece is two digits
walkthrough: Every reading ends with a one-digit or a two-digit piece. So the number of readings of the first i digits is the number of readings of the first i - 1 digits (if the last digit is a valid piece) plus the number of readings of the first i - 2 digits (if the last two digits are a valid piece).
• For "1", the digit 1 is valid, so there is 1 reading.
• For "11", the single 1 is valid (add 1) and the pair 11 is valid (add 1 from the empty prefix), so there are 2 readings.
• For "112", the single 2 is valid (add 2) and the pair 12 is valid (add 1), so there are 3 readings.
• For "1126", the single 6 is valid (add 3) and the pair 26 is valid (add 2), so there are 5 readings.
In "2105" the zero matters. At "210" the single 0 adds nothing, and the pair 10 adds the count for "2", which is 1. At "2105" the single 5 adds 1, and 05 is not a valid pair, so the answer is 1.
solution.timeWhy: One pass, checking one single digit and one pair per position.
solution.spaceWhy: Only the last two counts are kept.
solution.takeaway: When a string splits into pieces of a few possible lengths, count splits of each prefix from shorter prefixes, one term per possible last piece. The validity checks on that last piece carry all the tricky rules.
